# Zoost

> A small family of Chrome extensions (Manifest V3), one per Zoho product. Each mirrors what *you*
> have built inside that product into plain files on your own disk, then layers navigation, diagrams,
> search, an audit, exports and an optional AI assistant on top of that mirror. None of them writes
> anything back to Zoho. Everything runs in the browser; there is no server and no account.

This file exists so that an assistant sent to zoost.it can reach every claim the site makes **and the
evidence for it**, rather than summarising the marketing page. Every statement below is checkable, and
the last section says which ones cannot be checked and why.

## The two products

- [Zoost — workbench for Zoho CRM](https://zoost.it/crm.html): mirrors Deluge functions, module
  schema, layouts, related lists, workflows, schedules and the connections catalogue. Adds a
  reference graph, an ER diagram, full-text search across every function, a health audit, HTML and
  Markdown exports, and an optional AI assistant.
- [Zoost — workbench for Zoho Analytics](https://zoost.it/analytics.html): mirrors every view with
  its type and folder, the columns of every table and query table, the foreign keys between them, the
  SQL of each query table as its own file, and the dependency graph. Adds an ER diagram, a list of
  what nothing depends on any more, exports, and the same assistant.

## How to use them

- [How to use Zoost CRM](https://zoost.it/docs-crm.html)
- [How to use Zoost Analytics](https://zoost.it/docs-analytics.html)
- [Which guide you want](https://zoost.it/how-to.html)
- [The nerd page](https://zoost.it/nerd.html) - which endpoints, what breaks it, how a release is
  built and signed, and what none of that proves. The product pages point at it rather than
  carrying it, so this is where the technical claims live.

## What they do not do

Stated here rather than buried, because it is the part an assessment needs.

- **No write path to Zoho.** Neither extension calls an endpoint that creates, edits or deletes a
  function, a view, a record or a setting. Note the precise claim: this is a property of *which*
  endpoints are called, not something the browser enforces, and every call either makes is in
  about twenty readable files. One Zoho Analytics endpoint is a POST whose URL contains `CREATE` -
  `ZDBCreateERD.ma`, the call that returns the workspace's ER model. It computes; it does not
  create. It is named here because a reader checking the claim will find it.
- **They never read customer records.** Zoho CRM: no contacts, no deals, no notes - only the
  definitions of what you built. Zoho Analytics: never the rows inside a table; the endpoints that
  would return cell values exist and are deliberately never called.
- **Report definitions in Zoho Analytics are not covered.** Chart type, groupings and thresholds
  would require an endpoint that returns the computed data with them, so it is not called and the
  gap is stated wherever a report is shown.
- **Nothing leaves the machine except through the optional AI assistant**, which is off until the
  user supplies their own API key, and then talks only to Anthropic or OpenAI - the only two origins
  the manifest grants. Nothing is ever sent to the developer; there is no telemetry.
- **The API key is stored in clear text by default, and the product says so rather than implying
  otherwise.** Chrome offers extensions no encryption at rest and no credential store, so a key the
  extension can unlock by itself is one anyone with the browser profile can unlock. A passphrase the
  user chooses is offered as an opt-in (PBKDF2-SHA256 then AES-GCM-256, from the browser's own Web
  Crypto), leaving only ciphertext on disk and holding the unlocked key in session memory. There is
  no recovery, and the limit is stated where the choice is made: it protects the key at rest, not a
  key already unlocked in a running browser.
- **"Unused" is a candidate, never a verdict.** Both products state the coverage gap next to the
  number: a connection may be used by Zoho Flow or a widget, a view by a shared link or an API
  consumer, and neither platform reports that.
- **Counts are exposed, never graded.** Size and call counts come with what they do not capture, and
  there is no score, threshold or "worst offenders" list anywhere.

## Verifying the claims rather than believing them

- [Source](https://github.com/ivannot/zoost) - Apache-2.0. Around twenty files of plain JavaScript
  and HTML per extension. No bundler, no minifier, no dependencies, so what is published is what is
  in the repository and there is no build step that could add anything.
- [RELEASES.md](https://github.com/ivannot/zoost/blob/main/RELEASES.md) - every version submitted to
  the Chrome Web Store with its tag, commit and the SHA-256 of the uploaded archive. It also records
  what it *cannot* prove, including versions that predate the reproducible build.
- [The release workflow](https://github.com/ivannot/zoost/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yml) -
  pushing a tag makes GitHub check out that commit, build it twice to prove the bytes are
  deterministic, publish the archive and sign a provenance attestation. Every action is pinned to a
  commit hash. The build log is public.
- Check an archive against that record without trusting anyone:
  `gh attestation verify zoost-crm-<version>-store.zip --repo ivannot/zoost`
  and `tools/verify.sh crm <version>`, which rebuilds it from the tag and compares.
- [Privacy policy](https://zoost.it/privacy.html) - what is stored, where, and what leaves.

## What the product rests on

An assessment should have this before the verification chain, not after it.

- **Undocumented interfaces.** Zoho publishes no API for most of what Zoost reads, so both extensions
  use the same internal endpoints the products' own web interfaces use, through the session the user
  is already signed in to. The Zoho CRM one also reads the org id and user id out of the page's HTML,
  because nothing exposes them, and takes the CSRF token from the cookies the browser already holds.
  Separately it watches that page for one thing only: the URL and method of the request that saves a
  function, so the local copy can follow. It reads no headers and no response bodies, and alters
  nothing the page sends or receives.
- **Which means it can break.** Those interfaces carry no compatibility promise. Zoho can change one
  without notice and a feature can stop working from one day to the next.
- **What is promised.** Nothing is guaranteed; the licence says so. What is offered is effort - a
  break will be looked at and fixed where fixing it is possible, and where it is not, the feature
  will say it cannot do the thing rather than guess. The mirror already written to disk keeps working
  regardless, because it is ordinary files.

## What none of that proves

- Google repackages and re-signs every extension, so what the Chrome Web Store serves is not
  byte-identical to what was uploaded. The chain covers the input to that step; the far end is
  checked by unpacking the installed extension and diffing it against the tag.
- Uploading to the Store is a manual step and no signature covers it.
- An attestation says who built a file, never that the file is good. That part is reading the code,
  and nothing removes it.
- Reproducibility is verified on two environments (Info-ZIP 3.0 on macOS, and CI on ubuntu-latest),
  not asserted for every machine.
